text: Thomas had been married to Elaine for thirty-four years, and for most of them he assumed the marriage ran on routine. They argued about the thermostat. She kept a list of his doctor's appointments on the fridge, and he pretended not to read it. Then in January the biopsy came back, and for three weeks the house was quiet in a new way. He caught himself watching her across the kitchen as if she were a long-distance call that might drop. On the night of the surgery he sat in the parking garage for forty minutes before he could make himself go up. When the nurse finally let him in, Elaine was half asleep, her hair flattened on one side, and she asked whether he had eaten. He hadn't. She told him to get the soup from the cafeteria, the one with the bad crackers, and he laughed because it was so exactly her. He loved her in a way he had never bothered to put into words, since the words had always seemed unnecessary. Now he wanted to say all of them. Over the following months he learned to cut her grapefruit the way she liked, to sit through the dreadful mystery shows, to stop pretending he didn't notice when she was tired. Love, he decided, was mostly a matter of attention, and he finally paid it.

Throwaway account. I'm 36, married nine years, two kids under six. Posting because I don't know who else to tell. My husband Kofi has worked night shifts at the freight depot for four years so I could finish my nursing degree. Last week I came home from a double and found him asleep on the kitchen floor with the baby on his chest, both of them snoring, a bottle of formula tipped over beside them. I didn't wake them. I sat down on the tile and just watched. I love him so much it's almost embarrassing.

People talk about marriage like it's about big gestures, but mine is this: he's the one who knows I can't stand cilantro and picks it out of every dish before I notice. He drove forty minutes in the snow when my car died. He has never once made me feel guilty about the loans. Last night I told him I loved him for no reason at all, and he said, "I know, you tell me every day," and I cried into the dish towel. Is it weird that I still get butterflies after nine years? Honestly asking.

Also please tell me how to get formula out of a rug.

Dear Nadia,

You asked me last month whether I regret moving across the country to be near Dad's care home, and I didn't answer properly. The honest answer is no. Not because the days are easy, they aren't, but because every Tuesday I sit with him while he watches cricket highlights and tells me the same story about the cargo ship in Mombasa. I love him more now than I did when he was the man who came home late and smelled of diesel and ironing starch.

I know you feel guilty for living in Toronto. Please don't. You send him crossword books and photographs of the kids, and he reads them aloud to the nurses like they're scripture. That is love too, and it counts.

Come in April if you can. Bring the boys. He will pretend not to be thrilled, then ask them forty questions about football.

All my love, always,
Priya

March 3. Clear night, the first mild one. Drove out to the lake with the windows down and didn't turn on the radio. Ben had the thermos ready before I got my boots on, the cheap one with the dent, and he'd packed the good crackers, which he only does when he's trying hard.

Showed him the used fishing reel I bought off the guy in Yarrow. He examined it under the porch light for ten minutes, asked two questions I couldn't answer, and said it was a steal. Then he said it again, more quietly, like he wasn't sure I'd heard.

We sat on the dock until the frogs started. He told me about his sister's divorce, the parts she didn't say on the phone. I held his hand on the cold plank between us and didn't say anything clever. For once that felt right.

Drove home past the closed bowling alley. Ben fell asleep with his head against the window. At the driveway I didn't wake him right away. I sat there with the engine ticking and the porch light on, counting the seconds before he stirred.

Grace Kowalczyk's husband had been a long-haul trucker for twenty-two years, which meant she had learned to sleep on her side of the bed with one arm stretched across the empty space. When his route changed in the spring and he started coming home every night, she didn't know what to do with him. She reorganized the spice rack twice. She burned the first dinner he cooked for her. He stood in the kitchen doorway watching her scrape the pan, then came over and took the spatula out of her hand without a word. Their daughter asked why they were always touching now. Grace didn't know how to answer, so she said they were practicing. That night she lay awake listening to him breathe, a sound she had missed more than she'd admitted, and counted his breaths the way she used to count highway mileposts. In June they drove to the coast with the windows down and the radio off. He sang badly, and she didn't mind. At a gas station in Oregon he bought her a plastic keychain shaped like a lighthouse and handed it over with the seriousness of a jeweler. She clipped it to her purse and kept it there for years.
